entry.title: Listen Now crashed when two recents shared an id
entry.summary: In ShoutKit, Listen Now keyed Recently Played with Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues:). That initializer traps when two keys match. stationID stopped being unique in schema V2, because CloudKit does not support unique attributes, and with iCloud sync on the same station can briefly have two Recently Played rows. Drawing Listen Now in that window crashed. The change is shoutkit#288 (fa434a1), for shoutkit#282.
entry.content:
In ShoutKit, Listen Now keyed Recently Played with Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues:). That initializer traps when two keys match. stationID stopped being unique in schema V2, because CloudKit does not support unique attributes, and with iCloud sync on the same station can briefly have two Recently Played rows. Drawing Listen Now in that window crashed. The change is shoutkit#288 (fa434a1), for shoutkit#282.

The lookup trapped

displayedRecentStations built a dictionary from every recent row:

let byID = Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues: recents.map { ($0.stationID, $0) })

A duplicate stationID is a precondition failure, so Listen Now fatal-errored and Recently Played never appeared.

The store itself never inserts a second row for a station. mergeDuplicateStations() runs when the store is created, and the normal play path updates one row, so a single device that only writes through LibraryStore should not hit this. Two devices can each record the same station before they sync, and both rows then arrive. The crash is the gap after that import lands and before the next merge, while the view is on screen. logRecent kept the gap open: it updated matches.first and left the other row.

Show the latest play

RecentStation.latestByStationID(_:) builds the same lookup with Dictionary(_:uniquingKeysWith:) and keeps the row with the later playedAt:

static func latestByStationID(_ recents: some Sequence<RecentStation>) -> [String: RecentStation] {
    Dictionary(recents.map { ($0.stationID, $0) }) { first, second in
        first.playedAt >= second.playedAt ? first : second
    }
}

mergeDuplicateRecents() sorts by playedAt descending and keeps the first row it sees for each id, then adds the other play counts onto that row. The lookup picks that same survivor, so the view shows the row it will show after the merge. The view calls it:

// Not `uniqueKeysWithValues`: since schema version 2 two rows can
// share a station until they are merged (DECISIONS.md 2026-11-22).
let byID = RecentStation.latestByStationID(recents)
return recentlyPlayedTeaser.displayedIDs.compactMap { byID[$0] }

The function lives in Persistence. BrowseFeature depends on DesignSystem and cannot be tested on the Mac host, so this one-line call site in ListenNowView is untested.

Playing again merges the counts

logRecent collapses every row for the station before it writes the new play. collapseRecents keeps the latest playedAt, adds the others' playCount, and deletes the rest without saving:

func collapseRecents(_ recents: [RecentStation]) -> RecentStation? {
    guard let keeper = recents.max(by: { $0.playedAt < $1.playedAt }) else { return nil }
    for recent in recents where recent !== keeper {
        keeper.playCount += recent.playCount
        context.delete(recent)
    }
    return keeper
}

The keeper then records this play and takes the station's name:

if let existing = collapseRecents(matches) {
    existing.playedAt = .now
    existing.playCount += 1
    // A genuine new play un-hides it from Listen Now even if it was
    // previously dismissed there.
    existing.isHiddenFromListenNow = false
    existing.name = station.name

The test inserts the duplicates after the store has already merged at creation, saves, and then logs a play of KEXP:

// Arrive after the store merged at creation, as a sync import would.
context.insert(RecentStation(
    stationID: "kexp", name: "Older", genre: "", playedAt: Date(timeIntervalSince1970: 1000), playCount: 3,
))
context.insert(RecentStation(
    stationID: "kexp", name: "Newer", genre: "", playedAt: Date(timeIntervalSince1970: 2000), playCount: 2,
))

store.logRecent(Station(id: "kexp", name: "KEXP", genre: "Eclectic", listenerCount: 0))

One row remains, named KEXP, with play count 6. That is the older row's 3, the newer row's 2, and the new play.

#expect(recents.count == 1)
#expect(recents.first?.name == "KEXP")
#expect(recents.first?.playCount == 6)

A second test runs latestByStationID on two rows with station id kexp (named Old and New) and one named WFMU, in both orders. Both expect two entries, kexp pointing at New, and wfmu pointing at WFMU.

swift test --disable-xctest in Packages/Persistence reported 113 tests in 15 suites passed. xcodebuild with -destination 'generic/platform=iOS Simulator', CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO, and build-for-testing compiled the ListenNowView change. SwiftLint 0.65.1 --strict and SwiftFormat 0.64.5 --lint were clean. The simulator test plan was not run: that machine has no iOS Simulator runtime installed, and CI covers the plan. Nothing here was run on hardware. The issue did not need it.

What I would repeat

  • uniqueKeysWithValues traps on a duplicate key. After schema V2, two RecentStation rows can share an id between a sync import and mergeDuplicateStations(). A lookup built with that initializer crashes if Listen Now draws in the gap.
  • Keep the latest playedAt. Dictionary(_:uniquingKeysWith:) returns the later play, the same row mergeDuplicateRecents() keeps, so the teaser shows the row the merge will leave.
  • Add the other play counts on the write. collapseRecents sums them onto that row and deletes the rest. The test's counts are 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

entry.title: Pillow's convert() kept the camera GPS on the published original
entry.summary: In Bauhaus, embed_exif started from image.getexif() and only overwrote title, artist, and copyright. Image.convert("RGB") keeps the source EXIF, so /api/<date>/original was published with the camera's GPS IFD, body serial number, and maker notes. That is the file the Atom feed links as "Original". Unsplash photos, which the scheduled run uses when both museum sources fail, commonly carry GPS. The change is bauhaus#200 (7be86a6).
entry.content:
In Bauhaus, embed_exif started from image.getexif() and only overwrote title, artist, and copyright. Image.convert("RGB") keeps the source EXIF, so /api/<date>/original was published with the camera's GPS IFD, body serial number, and maker notes. That is the file the Atom feed links as "Original". Unsplash photos, which the scheduled run uses when both museum sources fail, commonly carry GPS. The change is bauhaus#200 (7be86a6).

The JPEG was not on the allowlist

The metadata JSON was already an allowlist that drops GPS. The JPEG was not. A client that asked for the privacy-safe image and a client that fetched the original were not looking at the same promise.

embed_exif copied the image's own directory and wrote three fields over it:

exif = image.getexif()

I reproduced that. convert("RGB") on a JPEG with a GPS IFD and BodySerialNumber still returned both.

The landscape gate scored the stored raster

A portrait stored as a landscape raster with Orientation=6 was measured by raw pixels, so it passed landscapes_only and would have been published as a wallpaper. Dropping the orientation tag without rotating the pixels would show that photo sideways.

Start from an empty EXIF directory

Published JPEGs now start from an empty directory and embed only title, artist, and copyright:

exif = Image.Exif()

open_rgb in src/quality.py applies EXIF orientation to the pixels before style transfer, the quality gate, and the published original. The landscape gate scores those upright dimensions. The source Orientation tag is no longer copied into metadata.json. Orientation was added to the deliberately omitted tag set next to BodySerialNumber, LensSerialNumber, and CameraOwnerName:

_DELIBERATELY_OMITTED = frozenset({
    "BodySerialNumber", "LensSerialNumber", "CameraOwnerName", "Orientation",
})

open_rgb loads the bytes, applies ImageOps.exif_transpose, then converts to RGB. convert() may return the same object, so the helper copies when that RGB image is the source or the oriented image. The copy survives the source being closed:

with Image.open(BytesIO(image_bytes)) as img:
    img.load()
    oriented = ImageOps.exif_transpose(img) or img
    rgb = oriented.convert("RGB")
    # convert() may return the same object. Copy so the result survives
    # the source image being closed.
    if rgb is img or rgb is oriented:
        rgb = rgb.copy()
    return rgb

Already published releases are immutable, so this protects new days.

After the change the published JPEG keeps title and artist, contains neither the serial nor a GPS IFD, and an Orientation=6 raster of 1200x800 decodes as 800x1200. uv run pytest reported 314 passed and 4 skipped.

What I would repeat

  • convert() keeps EXIF. Writing title, artist, and copyright over image.getexif() leaves the GPS IFD, the body serial number, and the maker notes in place.
  • Start from an empty directory and allowlist. Image.Exif() plus those three fields is what the published JPEG carries. The JSON allowlist did not cover that file.
  • Bake orientation into the pixels first. Run ImageOps.exif_transpose before dropping the tag or measuring width and height. A 1200x800 raster with Orientation=6 is 800x1200 to a viewer.

entry.title: Don't parse show notes until something reads them
entry.summary: Podr turned every episode and podcast description that contained < or & into plain text with DOMParser on the main thread, during feed load, before the episode list could update. Ordinary notes are a string scan now. The plain text is computed the first time something reads description, and cached. Laziness beat a worker: the scan needs no DOM, copying a multi-megabyte feed across threads costs more than the scan, and the fallback needs DOMParser, which workers do not have. The change is podr#188 (10c3607). podr#186 left this open. Large descriptions were still parsed in full on the main thread.
entry.content:
Podr turned every episode and podcast description that contained < or & into plain text with DOMParser on the main thread, during feed load, before the episode list could update. Ordinary notes are a string scan now. The plain text is computed the first time something reads description, and cached. Laziness beat a worker: the scan needs no DOM, copying a multi-megabyte feed across threads costs more than the scan, and the fallback needs DOMParser, which workers do not have. The change is podr#188 (10c3607). podr#186 left this open. Large descriptions were still parsed in full on the main thread.

What I measured

The numbers are from jsdom, on show notes shaped like a CMS export: paragraphs, links, lists, WordPress comments, and the character references those tools emit (&, ’, —, “, é). The scanner's text matched DOMParser. The 300-episode run produced the same 1,502,260 characters.

Before (DOMParser)After
One 12,767-byte description6.9 ms0.32 ms
One 128,381-byte description42.4 ms1.7 ms
300 descriptions, 10,923 bytes each (3.31 MB)890 ms, during feed parse0.9 ms to parse the feed, then 4.0 ms for the first 30

The list mounts 30 rows. Those are the notes that used to be waited on along with the other 270. Reading all 300 with the scanner, for a case that does walk every episode, took 41 ms.

App JS is 17KB gzip. The previous review measured about 15KB, so the reader and its character-reference table are about 2KB.

Read it when something asks

A feed can carry hundreds of episodes. Scanning every show-notes string before the list paints blocks the main thread for notes the listener has not asked to see. description is a getter. Spread would read that getter immediately, so the property is defined on the object:

function defineLazyDescription<T extends object>(
  target: T,
  raw: string
): T & { readonly description: string } {
  return Object.defineProperty(target, 'description', {
    enumerable: true,
    get(): string {
      return raw ? toPlainText(raw) : '';
    },
  }) as T & { readonly description: string };
}

The list mounts a page of rows, and saving keeps a short prefix of the first sixty. Both read description and pay for those only. The value is the same plain text toPlainText has always returned.

toPlainText remembers 64 recent plain-text results. Opening a podcast reads each visible description once for the row and again when the trimmed copy is saved. The second read is the stored string:

const cached = plainTextCache.get(value);

if (cached !== undefined) {
  return rememberPlainText(value, cached);
}

A description that is the only field has to be read during the parse. Markup that leaves no text (<br>) is an empty result, the same as a missing description. When the feed already has a title, author, or image, the notes wait until the page shows them.

Hand the rest to DOMParser

readHtmlText in src/utils/htmlText.ts returns the text a document's body would expose for ordinary markup. Null means the fragment is outside what the scan claims. The caller then uses DOMParser, so the text stays the same.

const scanned = readHtmlText(prepared);

if (scanned !== null) {
  text = scanned;
} else {
  descriptionParser ??= new DOMParser();
  text = descriptionParser.parseFromString(prepared, 'text/html').body.textContent ?? '';
}

A space is inserted before br, /p, /div, /li, and heading closers before either reader runs. That space survives as text once the tag is gone, so adjacent paragraphs do not run together, and the two readers stay in agreement.

The scan refuses these tags, and any character reference it does not know completely:

const RAW_TAGS = new Set([
  'script',
  'style',
  'title',
  'template',
  'textarea',
  'xmp',
  'iframe',
  'noembed',
  'noframes',
  'plaintext',
  'svg',
  'math',
]);

Script, style, title, and template land in the document head, so their contents were never part of body.textContent. The scanner returns null for them instead of guessing, and toPlainText then matches the document:

expect(readHtmlText('<script>alert(1)</script>Shown')).toBeNull();
expect(readHtmlText('<style>p{}</style>Hi')).toBeNull();
expect(readHtmlText('<svg><text>icon</text></svg>')).toBeNull();
expect(readHtmlText('<p>Ordinary</p>')).toBe('Ordinary');

expect(toPlainText('<script>alert(1)</script>Shown as text')).toBe('Shown as text');
expect(toPlainText('<style>p{color:red}</style>Hi')).toBe('Hi');

DOMParser runs with scripting disabled. Scripts do not run and images do not load. <noscript> is ordinary markup in that mode, and its text is kept.

A name that is only a prefix of a real reference refuses the scan, so the HTML parser can apply the longest-match rule. &ere; stays &ere; rather than being guessed.

The comment on toPlainText says building a document per episode is what janks a feed of long show notes, and a worker cannot host DOMParser. Markup the string reader will not claim still goes through DOMParser. The scan itself needs no DOM, and copying a multi-megabyte feed across threads costs more than doing it here.

The two lines on screen stay in CSS

The full note is still what gets shown. The two-line clamp stays in CSS, so find-in-page and screen readers keep the rest. The long-notes fixture checks that the scan reads the tail:

// The tail is still there: the scan does not stop at the two lines on screen.
expect(text.endsWith('Episode 7.')).toBe(true);

An independent DOMParser is the oracle

The tests compare toPlainText with domPlainText, which calls DOMParser itself, including hostile markup. A faster reader cannot pass by being compared with itself.

text =
  new DOMParser().parseFromString(text.replace(blockBoundary, ' $&'), 'text/html').body
    .textContent ?? '';

A long show-notes fixture asserts the scanner does not call parseFromString. A feed of notes that do need the parser asserts nothing is parsed until description is read, and a second read does not parse again:

expect(parseFromString).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
expect(items[0].description).toBe('One');
expect(parseFromString).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
// The same episode's notes are already plain text.
expect(items[0].description).toBe('One');
expect(parseFromString).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

281 tests passed, lint reported no new warnings, and the production build succeeded.

What I would repeat

  • Defer the parse. A visible row, the podcast header, or the offline short copy is what reads description. The other episodes can wait.
  • Return null when the scan would guess. Script and style contents stay out because the document puts those elements in the head. The scanner refuses the tags and DOMParser does the omission.
  • Leave the clamp in CSS. Cutting the note while parsing would take it away from find-in-page and screen readers.
  • Skip the worker when the fallback needs DOM. The copy of a multi-megabyte feed costs more than this scan, and a worker has no DOMParser.

entry.title: The Same Audit on a Second Game Found More: Salt Line's Solver in 40 Percent of the Time
entry.summary: Yesterday I wrote about making my racing game's track solver a third faster without changing one answer. Salt Line, its artillery sibling, has the same kind of prover, so I ran the same audit on it.
entry.content:
Yesterday I wrote about making my racing game's track solver a third faster without changing one answer. Salt Line, its artillery sibling, has the same kind of prover, so I ran the same audit on it.

It came out better. The proof now takes about 40 percent of the time it did. It accepts the same screens, lists the same shots and reports the same flight times as before, bit for bit.

The Short Version

BeforeAfter
Batch of 5,000 screens, one thread10.4–11.2 s4.1–4.2 s
Generation gate, 4,000 screens0.800 s0.316 s
Prove one screen solvable28–109 µs11–48 µs
Generate one screen, proof included59–163 µs31–69 µs
Resolve one shot925 ns566 ns
Solver resultsidentical

Those are from one pinned core of a 4-core x86-64 cloud machine, release build. The machine is noisy, so read the ratios and not the third digit. I haven't measured a phone, or arm64 at all.

What "Proven" Costs

Salt Line never shows a screen it hasn't proven clearable. For each target, a solver sweeps forty flight times, solves each for the angle and power that would land there, and snaps the answer to what the player's dials can actually set. Then it flies every candidate through the game's own fixed-step integrator and applies the game's own damage code, because the closed form knows nothing about wind changes, ricochets or tunnelling. A screen needs three distinct shots per target. One that fails is redrawn, down a ladder that ends on level ground.

The sim is deterministic across Linux, macOS, Windows and phones, and a daily seed has to be the same game for everyone. So the rule was the same as last time: a speed-up that moves one result is a bug, not a trade-off.

Save the Answers Before the First Edit

Before I touched anything, I saved everything that prints a solver result:

  • the batch reports, for the default build and each of the five build shapes
  • the balance reports and the salvage probe
  • both determinism runs, with all 200 run hashes
  • a throwaway dump of 57,675 lines: for 75 loadouts, the screen hash, the rung, and every candidate's shot with the exact bits of its flight times, on fresh screens and again after three shots of damage

The batch report had no per-screen detail, so I wrote the dump for the audit. After every change I ran all twelve files again and diffed them, ignoring one timing line.

Where the Time Went

In the generation gate, 89 percent was the solver and 11 percent was building terrain. Inside the solver, 77 percent was flights, which I expected. I didn't expect this: 36 percent of the whole run was flying shots the solver had just flown.

Fewer Ticks

Don't fly the same shot twice

The solver flew each candidate once to see whether it landed anywhere near the target. If it did, it handed the shot to the game's damage code on a scratch copy of the screen, so the proof could never drift from what the game does. That code flew the shot again.

The copy is identical to the screen until the damage is applied, and a flight depends only on the screen, the shot, the loadout and the fuse. The second flight could only repeat the first. I split "fire a shot" into "fly it" and "apply what flew" and gave the copy the flight the solver already had. That one change took about 45 percent off the full candidate count.

Don't find every answer to use one

The attract demo, the autopilot and the challenge hint arcs all asked the solver for every shot that fells a target, then used the first. There can be over a hundred. The search visits shots in the same order whatever the limit, so stopping at the first gives the same shot. That went from about 600 µs to between 2 and 13 µs.

Cheaper Ticks

The same floor

The terrain lookup under the shell called floor on every step, and on x86-64 without SSE4.1 that's a library call. By the time the lookup reaches it, the position is known to be positive and inside the field, where truncating is the floor. Same lead as the racing game, same fix.

Boxes the shell is nowhere near

Every step was swept against every target's box. Most steps are far from all of them. Skipping those took another fifth off the full count, and it was the one change I couldn't make the easy way. More on that below.

Trig on 1,801 angles

The barrel has 1,801 positions. The solver's angle search asked for the sine and cosine of the same ones several thousand times per screen. They now come from a table that's filled on first use by the same computation.

The same two hashes

Terrain noise hashed two lattice values for every sample. The terrain is sampled once per pixel column and a lattice cell is tens to hundreds of columns wide, so nearly every sample hashed the pair the one before it had. Each noise layer now remembers its last pair. A hash is a pure function of its inputs, so the remembered value is the value.

The Change That Wasn't Obviously Safe

Skipping the box sweep sounds trivial. If a step is outside the bounding box of all the boxes, it can't hit one.

In exact arithmetic that's true. In floating point it isn't quite. The segment test divides two rounded differences, and for a step that ends within a rounding error of a box edge it can report a hit that exact arithmetic wouldn't. A plain bounding-box check would disagree with it there. It would be vanishingly rare, and it would break the rule.

So the skip only applies when both ends of the step are more than one unit clear of every box, and every number involved is below 2⁴⁰. With that much room, the segment test's own first failing clip has to reject the step: the two differences can't round to the same value, and the quotient can't underflow to zero. The argument is in a comment beside the code. A test checks it against the real segment test on the edges and their neighbouring floats, on NaN and infinities, and on 360,000 ordinary steps.

The Bug My Own Test Found

In the racing game, removing waste exposed an old bug. Here the bug was mine.

My first draft of the terrain lookup panicked on a NaN position over a one-column field, where the old code returned NaN. Nothing in the game can produce that input. The test that compares the new lookup to the old one on awkward values produced it anyway, and the rule has no exception for inputs I think are impossible.

What I Threw Away

Each of these looked good in the profiler and failed on the stopwatch.

  • A hand-written floor with no library call removed 6.5 percent of instructions and no measurable time over forty runs.
  • Inlining the terrain lookup was lost in the noise.
  • Skipping the ground test when the shell is above all terrain made the run about 50 percent slower. Finding the highest ground for each shell cost more than the tests it saved.

What I Left Alone

Nothing was reordered, no trial count or cap changed, and the solver is still single-threaded.

And as before, arm64 has a floor instruction, so the truncation will count for less on a phone. The rest doesn't care about the architecture.

What Doing It Twice Taught Me

  • The biggest win was the same kind of thing both times. Two pieces of code each did the careful thing without knowing the other had. A profiler finds that in minutes.
  • If the tool that prints your results has no detail, write one that does. I couldn't have trusted a summary histogram to notice one changed shot.
  • "Obviously equivalent" is a claim about real numbers. The bounding-box skip is true in maths and false in floats. A margin made it true in both.
  • Test the new form against the old on values you'd never pass. That's where mine differed.
  • Believe the stopwatch over the profiler. Two changes that removed instructions removed no time, and a third made the run slower.

entry.title: I shipped 11,105 icons to use 17
entry.summary: ShoutKit's phone app draws 31 Material icons, and the watch app draws three: PlayArrow, Pause, and Stop. Fourteen of the phone's icons come from material-icons-core. The other seventeen came from material-icons-extended. The 1.7.8 Android archive of that library is 11,105 icon classes. Release builds shrink the unused ones away. Debug builds dex every class, and that step is where CI ran out of heap. Copying the seventeen and dropping the dependency took the FOSS debug APK from 29,397,070 bytes to 22,728,773.
entry.content:
ShoutKit's phone app draws 31 Material icons, and the watch app draws three: PlayArrow, Pause, and Stop. Fourteen of the phone's icons come from material-icons-core. The other seventeen came from material-icons-extended. The 1.7.8 Android archive of that library is 11,105 icon classes. Release builds shrink the unused ones away. Debug builds dex every class, and that step is where CI ran out of heap. Copying the seventeen and dropping the dependency took the FOSS debug APK from 29,397,070 bytes to 22,728,773.

The phone app turns minify and resource shrinking on for the release build type only:

release {
    isMinifyEnabled = true
    isShrinkResources = true

Debug leaves both at the Android Gradle Plugin default, so the dex step sees every icon in the dependency.

Where the heap went

A push on #342 failed two jobs. The build died with Error while dexing on material-icons-extended, in :app:mergeExtDexPlayDebug and :cast:mergeExtDexPlayDebug. CodeQL's autobuild died with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Both passed on a rerun. The Gradle heap was 4 GB. #343 raised org.gradle.jvmargs to -Xmx6g and set kotlin.daemon.jvmargs=-Xmx3g, so the Kotlin compile daemon, a second JVM, fits a 16 GB runner alongside Gradle. The icon library stayed. That write-up called it about 11,000 icons, of which the app used 32, and left the replacement for a later change.

The removal counted 31 on the phone and 3 on the watch. material-icons-extended-android 1.7.8 contains 11,105 classes, one val Icons property each: 2,083 names in each of filled, outlined, rounded, sharp, and twotone, and 138 automirrored icons in each of those styles. None of those names are the fourteen the phone imports from core. Compose BOM 2026.09.00, the version in the catalog, still resolves both icon artifacts to 1.7.8, and 1.7.8 is the latest release on Google's Maven repository. The metadata was last updated on 2025-02-12. The POM says the module is a very large dependency and should not be included directly.

The seventeen copies

#345 (9703448) removes material-icons-extended from the phone app, the watch app, and the version catalog. The watch module depends on material-icons-core on its own. The seventeen icons are copied from the 1.7.8 sources into com.cascadiacollections.sir.ui.icons: Backup, Bedtime, ContentCopy, DragHandle, FileDownload, FileUpload, FilterList, GraphicEq, History, LibraryMusic, MusicNote, Pause, PlayCircle, QueueMusic, Radio, Stop, and WifiOff. Sixteen are Icons.Filled. QueueMusic is Icons.AutoMirrored.Filled, the variant the library screen already used. Pause and Stop are copied again into com.cascadiacollections.sir.wear.icons, because the two apps share no Compose code. The watch's third icon, PlayArrow, stays on core. Call sites keep writing Icons.Default (an alias for Icons.Filled) and Icons.AutoMirrored.Filled, and change the import. The phone app drops the extended dependency and keeps core:

implementation(libs.androidx.compose.material.icons.core)

The fourteen that stay on core are Add, ArrowBack (automirrored), Check, Clear, Close, Delete, Favorite, FavoriteBorder, MoreVert, PlayArrow, Refresh, Search, Settings, and Share.

Under the Apache-2.0 header, Pause says where it came from and what changed:

// Copied from androidx.compose.material:material-icons-extended 1.7.8, package
// androidx.compose.material.icons.filled, so the app can use this icon without depending
// on the whole library. Changes from the original: the package, no explicit `public`,
// and the lint suppression below (the cache field's name is upstream's).
@file:Suppress("BackingPropertyNaming")

val Icons.Filled.Pause: ImageVector

REUSE.toml marks both directories Apache-2.0, so those terms stay on the copies inside the GPL-3.0 apps:

# Material icons copied from androidx.compose.material:material-icons-extended 1.7.8, so the
# apps ship the 17 icons they use instead of the whole library. Apache-2.0, as each file's
# header says; they keep those terms inside the GPL-3.0 apps.
[[annotations]]
path = [
    "app/src/main/java/com/cascadiacollections/sir/ui/icons/**",
    "wear/src/main/java/com/cascadiacollections/sir/wear/icons/**",
]
precedence = "override"
SPDX-FileCopyrightText = "The Android Open Source Project"
SPDX-License-Identifier = "Apache-2.0"

What the clean build measured

The commit message says the FOSS debug APK went from 35.1 MB to 22.7 MB. #345 measured both sides clean, ff30d27 on main against the branch, each with --rerun-tasks --no-build-cache. The before size in that run is 29,397,070 bytes. The 35.1 MB figure came from an incremental build.

BeforeAfter
FOSS debug APK29,397,070 B22,728,773 B
Debug dex, uncompressed85.2 MB54.0 MB
Methods defined in the debug APK236,017213,150
androidx.compose.material.icons methods23,529 (13.7 MB of dex)628 (0.25 MB)
Release APK4,278,226 B4,278,226 B

The release APK is the same 4,278,226 bytes. R8 was already removing the unused icons, so the bytes that moved are in the debug APK, which is what CI dexes. The debug APK is 6,668,297 bytes smaller, 22.7%. One clean debug build was a little faster, 78.7 s to 71.0 s with a cold daemon and 21.4 s to 19.6 s warm. Those are one run each.

detekt, :app:lintPlayDebug, :wear:lintDebug, :app:testFossDebugUnitTest, :wear:testDebugUnitTest, :app:assembleFossDebug, and :wear:assembleDebug passed locally, and so did reuse lint and .github/scripts/check-license-boundary.sh. The vectors are the 1.7.8 paths. A side-by-side look on a device is still open, and the watch app was only compiled.

The 6 GB heap from #343 is still in gradle.properties. The dex that ran out of memory was this library. If a debug build is dexing material-icons-extended to draw a handful of icons, copy those icons and keep material-icons-core.

entry.title: Getting the test-results comment back without checks: write
entry.summary: deathban-pro#83 removed EnricoMi/publish-unit-test-result-action from CI. The workflow had granted checks: write at the top, and OpenSSF Scorecard's Token-Permissions check warns on that scope, including when only a job sets it. The pull-request comment went away with the action. deathban-pro#87 puts a comment back from a later job whose write scope is pull-requests: write.
entry.content:
deathban-pro#83 removed EnricoMi/publish-unit-test-result-action from CI. The workflow had granted checks: write at the top, and OpenSSF Scorecard's Token-Permissions check warns on that scope, including when only a job sets it. The pull-request comment went away with the action. deathban-pro#87 puts a comment back from a later job whose write scope is pull-requests: write.

What the publish step needed

The build job used to publish results itself:

- name: Publish test results
  uses: EnricoMi/publish-unit-test-result-action@v2
  if: always()
  with:
    files: build/test-results/test/*.xml
    check_name: Test Results
    comment_mode: always

Above that job the workflow permissions were contents: read, checks: write, and pull-requests: write. The step sets check_name: Test Results, so the token has to create a check run. After #83 the top of .github/workflows/ci.yml is contents: read, and that step is gone.

A separate job

The build job still runs Gradle, on that read-only token. After the tests it uploads build/test-results/test/*.xml as an artifact named junit-xml, and it appends the same counts to the job summary. The summary is GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY. It needs no extra scope, so a fork, Dependabot, and a push to main still show the counts on the run.

The comment is the test-results job, as merged in d174f05. It waits for build. It runs for a same-repo pull request that is not from Dependabot, when the build succeeded or failed:

# One comment for same-repo pull requests. The build job stays read-only.
# Scorecard v5.7 (scorecard-action v2.6.0) warns when the checks scope is
# write, including at job level, and does not treat pull-requests write as
# one of those scopes. Fork and Dependabot tokens cannot write from this
# event; pr-test-results.yml comments for those after CI completes.
test-results:
  name: Test result comment
  needs: build
  if: >-
    always() &&
    github.event_name == 'pull_request' &&
    github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository &&
    github.actor != 'dependabot[bot]' &&
    (needs.build.result == 'success' || needs.build.result == 'failure')
  runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
  timeout-minutes: 5
  permissions:
    actions: read
    contents: read
    pull-requests: write
  steps:
    - name: Checkout
      uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      with:
        persist-credentials: false

    - name: Download JUnit XML
      continue-on-error: true
      uses: actions/download-artifact@37930b1c2abaa49bbe596cd826c3c89aef350131 # v7.0.0
      with:
        name: junit-xml
        path: junit-xml

    - name: Publish pull request comment
      env:
        GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        GITHUB_REPOSITORY: ${{ github.repository }}
        PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
        HEAD_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
        RUN_URL: ${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}
        RESULTS_DIR: junit-xml
        BUILD_RESULT: ${{ needs.build.result }}
      run: python3 scripts/test_results_comment.py post

actions: read is the artifact download. contents: read is the checkout. pull-requests: write is the comment.

What Scorecard v5.7 counts

.github/workflows/scorecard.yml pins ossf/scorecard-action to 23f22cd43608bae7a1f1fa2603d7314dee9538a5 (v2.6.0). That tag's go.mod requires github.com/ossf/scorecard/v5 v5.7.0.

In checks/raw/permissions.go the writes that count are statuses, checks, security-events, deployments, contents, packages, and actions. A write of one of those is recorded at the top of the file and on a job. checks/evaluation/permissions.go warns when a job sets one of them to write. checks: write on the job that creates the check run is still that warning, so the publish action does not fit there either.

pull-requests is absent from that list. The raw check stores the write as a non-dangerous write, and the score does not drop for it.

Run 45500072078 is Scorecard v5.7.0 on the merge commit. Token-Permissions logged the comment job as Info: jobLevel 'actions' permission set to 'read': .github/workflows/ci.yml:199 and the same for contents on line 200, then Info: no jobLevel write permissions found. Line 201 is pull-requests: write, and it is absent from that log. The check still scored 0, on a warning that was already there: Warn: topLevel 'contents' permission set to 'write': .github/workflows/release.yml:14. #87 leaves release.yml alone.

The Scorecard job on the pull request head never printed a score. Run 45453315532 failed pulling ghcr.io/ossf/scorecard-action:v2.6.0 with manifest unknown.

The checkout and the one comment

The comment job runs on its own runner. Its checkout leaves ref unset, so the files are the commit that the workflow run is executing, and it sets persist-credentials: false. The XML it reads is the junit-xml artifact uploaded by build. The Gradle job keeps the read-only token.

scripts/test_results_comment.py starts the body with <!-- deathban-pro-test-results -->. A later CI run edits the earliest github-actions[bot] comment that contains that marker, and deletes later bot copies of it. Comments from any other author stay put.

On #87 that is one comment. GitHub created it at 17:50 UTC and updated it at 17:54 UTC. The body shows 6f01d55cc66e, the second commit on the pull request, and links run 45453315718. CI ignores **/*.md, so a docs-only push does not run the job. The comment says it is updated when CI finishes.

Fork pull_request tokens stay read-only, and Dependabot tokens do too, even when the workflow file asks for write. The test-results job is skipped for them. .github/workflows/pr-test-results.yml runs on workflow_run after CI completes, from the default-branch copy of the workflow. It downloads the artifact, and its checkout also leaves ref unset. Same-repo runs that are not from Dependabot are skipped there, so those pull requests get the one comment from ci.yml. Dangerous-Workflow on the merge run scored 10: no dangerous workflow patterns detected.

A test report that can live as a pull-request comment can use pull-requests: write on its own job. checks: write is the scope Scorecard warns on, at the top of the workflow and on the job.

entry.title: The third draft card was pause, and the shell reserve could wrap
entry.summary: Two bugs in Salt Line, both reachable from ordinary play and both fixed in saltline#167 (d5d720c). On a controller the third draft card shared B with pause, and pause is the first thing play asks for, so the press opened the pause screen. The shell reserve is an i32 with no cap unless Forced March imposes one, and a Standing Orders streak pays a bonus that grows on every one-shot clear. Past i32::MAX that add panics in a debug build and wraps negative in a release build. A negative reserve is out of shells.
entry.content:
Two bugs in Salt Line, both reachable from ordinary play and both fixed in saltline#167 (d5d720c). On a controller the third draft card shared B with pause, and pause is the first thing play asks for, so the press opened the pause screen. The shell reserve is an i32 with no cap unless Forced March imposes one, and a Standing Orders streak pays a bonus that grows on every one-shot clear. Past i32::MAX that add panics in a debug build and wraps negative in a release build. A negative reserve is out of shells.

The press was taken by pause

A press is taken by the first action that asks for it. Two actions bound to the same button in the same mode never both fire. input.rs says the order the core asks in is part of the behaviour, and take_pad removes the press it reports.

handle_play_input asks for pause, then for a draft pick, then for aim and fire. Pause wins, and the function returns:

/// A run in play: pause, draft picks, then aim, fuse, reposition and fire.
pub(super) fn handle_play_input(&mut self, delta: f64) {
    if self.action_pressed(Action::Back) {
        self.input.touch.cancel_drag();
        self.mode = Mode::Paused;
        return;
    }

The draft ask is the next block, over Draft1, Draft2 and Draft3, and it returns too. Back's default pad button is B. Draft 3's was B too. Keys 1, 2 and 3, and a tap on the card, never went through that button.

Action::Draft1 => ("1", "X"),
Action::Draft2 => ("2", "A"),
Action::Draft3 => ("3", "B"),
Action::Back => ("ESCAPE", "B"),

Pad A is also fire. That one works: the draft is asked before fire, the pick is taken, and the function returns. Pad B lost, because pause is asked before the draft and the function returns there. The third offer stayed on the table, and the pause screen opened over a draft that was still open.

Draft 3 is now Y. The comment on the binding is the reason Y is free while a draft is up:

// Y, not B. Pause is B and is read before a draft pick, so a third
// offer bound to B never took: the press opened the pause screen.
// Y is free on the draft (reposition, replay and star read it on
// other screens).
Action::Draft3 => ("3", "Y"),

B still pauses. The settings screen used to show a draft as two buttons, one row of an action plus an optional second, so it listed X and A and left the third off. The draft row now carries all three actions, which with the defaults reads X/A/Y. With a controller in use, before the draft has been learned, the prompt is X A Y PICK A MODIFIER. A touchscreen still says TAP A CARD PICK A MODIFIER. The README row is 1 / 2 / 3, X / A / Y, tap a card, and B still pauses.

in_a_draft_pad_b_pauses_and_y_takes_the_third_card presses B, sees Mode::Paused with the phase still Drafting and zero stacks of the third offer, presses B again to resume, then presses Y. The loadout has that offer and the phase has left the draft.

The reserve stopped at the top of an i32

Loadout::cap is i32::MAX unless a modifier imposes one. Taking Forced March drops a reserve of 40 to 15 on the spot. The comment on cap keeps the default open on purpose: a 40-shell ceiling would eat most of a Depot on the first draft, and Depot, Storm Front and Quartermaster would stop being worth taking. Standing Orders reads "One-shot clears grant +1 per consecutive streak." The streak is a u32. A one-shot clear increments it and adds that count to the shells paid for the screen.

The old grant was a plain add, then the cap:

self.shells = (self.shells + n).min(self.loadout.cap());

and the streak was a plain increment, then a cast:

self.one_shot_streak += 1;
if self.loadout.standing_orders() {
    gain += self.one_shot_streak as i32;
}

i32 addition panics on overflow in debug and wraps in release. A reserve at or below zero is Phase::Over(RunOver::OutOfShells), checked when a shot fails to clear and again when the run advances after a clear. That is the only way a run ends. Casting a streak above i32::MAX wraps too, so the bonus itself could arrive negative. A streak already at u32::MAX wraps to 0 on += 1 in release, and panics in debug.

A debug panic is the error screen. The hook writes user://crash.txt, and the next frame draws SOMETHING BROKE / THE GAME STOPPED RATHER THAN CARRY ON WRONG. Anything that writes, moves or deletes a file is dropped after a panic, so the half-updated run is not saved over the last good one. The report is the last file that session writes.

Grants now saturate, then the cap still applies. The supply screen's +6 goes through grant too, instead of its own shells + 6. The streak saturates at u32::MAX, and the bonus is the streak as an i32, or i32::MAX when it does not fit:

fn grant(&mut self, n: i32) {
    // An uncapped reserve plus Standing Orders grows without a ceiling.
    // A wrapping add would panic in debug and, in release, turn a huge
    // reserve negative and end the run. Stop at `i32::MAX`, then apply
    // the cap (`i32::MAX` when nothing has imposed one).
    self.shells = self.shells.saturating_add(n).min(self.loadout.cap());
}

if shots <= 1 {
    // Saturating: a streak that has already reached `u32::MAX` must
    // not wrap, and the bonus paid below must not wrap to a negative
    // shell count.
    self.one_shot_streak = self.one_shot_streak.saturating_add(1);
    if self.loadout.standing_orders() {
        let bonus = i32::try_from(self.one_shot_streak).unwrap_or(i32::MAX);
        gain = gain.saturating_add(bonus);
    }
} else {
    self.one_shot_streak = 0;
}
self.grant(gain);

depot_grants_its_shells_once_on_take moves a reserve of 10 to 18, so that grant is 8 shells. the_reserve_stops_at_i32_max_instead_of_wrapping takes a Depot at i32::MAX - 1 and stops at i32::MAX. The old add would have overflowed there. a_huge_one_shot_streak_does_not_wrap_the_reserve starts from 20 shells with Standing Orders and one_shot_streak already u32::MAX, clears the screen in one shot, and expects i32::MAX shells, the streak still at u32::MAX, and the run not over.

The golden-run digest stayed

SIM_EPOCH versions the sim's outcomes. A change that alters a replay bumps it. tests/golden_runs.rs hashes the golden-run corpus and requires that epoch's digest. Epoch 6's is 0x0e22_2e08_a33e_af8a. This fix leaves the epoch at 6. Adds that stay inside the type are the same values as before, and the pull request records that the golden-run digest did not move.

Same standard as the track solver the same day. There, a faster proof was only allowed through if every timer and every failure stayed put, and a saved digest was the check.

The artillery digest is a different number from the Drone Trial digest. CI used to compare only the artillery one, so a replay break that existed only in the trial would still pass the matrix. saltline#173 runs trial_determinism in the sim job, the Android emulator job and the iOS simulator job, and uploads trial-digest-<platform>.txt beside the artillery file. The determinism job compares the two sets separately. Each set has to agree with itself: seven copies when the Apple jobs run, and fewer on a gameplay-only pull request, the same count the artillery set already uses.

The pull request records a local run, cargo run --release -q -p salt-line-sim --bin trial_determinism: 200 replays, 139 hits, zero divergences, digest: 0xff8e006571cf0da1, about five seconds. The Android emulator and the iOS simulator steps were left to CI. They spawn the second binary the same way they spawn the artillery digest. just android-digest on a phone still runs the artillery binary only. The emulator covers the trial on bionic.

entry.title: Don't flip the JVM flag, measure it on a copy of the world
entry.summary: JDK 25 can shrink object headers with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders. On the Paper server that can cut the heap, and it can also move GC pauses and tick time. I built a harness that copies the world twice and compares the two runs. I have not measured the world yet. The numbers come later.
entry.content:
JDK 25 can shrink object headers with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders. On the Paper server that can cut the heap, and it can also move GC pauses and tick time. I built a harness that copies the world twice and compares the two runs. I have not measured the world yet. The numbers come later.

The flag stays off

cdb170b made scripts/jvm-opts.sh the flag list for a host start and for the container image. With no container memory limit, that script boots on a safe default heap, about a quarter of host memory clamped between 1G and 4G, or 2G when host memory cannot be read. Compact headers stay out of that list. They sit outside Aikar's flags.

minecraft-server#133 (b15e353) adds the opt-in on top of that script, and the harness that has to pass before the flag is turned on for a server people play. scripts/jvm-opts.sh appends -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders only when COMPACT_OBJECT_HEADERS is true, 1, yes, or on. Any other value is an error. Unset, false, 0, no, and off leave it off. G1 already passes -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions. ZGC does not, so the opt-in adds that unlock only for ZGC. JDK 25 still treats the flag as experimental.

Compose JVM_XX_OPTS leaves the flag out. The custom image uses scripts/jvm-opts.sh, so the same variable is the opt-in there. The live server keeps the current flags. An ACCEPT from the harness is evidence for a follow-up. It leaves the default off.

Two copies, one difference

scripts/measure-compact-headers.sh copies the world with cp -a, once into baseline/world and once into compact/world, both from the original. The second run starts from the same files as the first. The server directory is always one of those copies, and server.properties sets level-name=world there.

Both runs call scripts/jvm-opts.sh with MEMORY_MODE=fixed and the same heap, GC, and dump settings. The compact run is the only one with COMPACT_OBJECT_HEADERS=true. Before Java starts, the script stops if the baseline flags mention UseCompactObjectHeaders, and it stops if the compact flags are missing the line -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders. Each run adds the same -Xlog:gc* options, with a different log path. HeapDumpPath differs by run directory.

Defaults match a host start: G1, -Xms4G -Xmx4G, view distance 10, simulation distance 10. The measurement server listens on 127.0.0.1:25566, with an empty plugins directory, peaceful difficulty, mob spawning off, and pause-when-empty-seconds=-1. After Paper prints Done, it waits 120 seconds, then samples for 180 seconds. The runs are sequential, so one heap is touched at a time, and AlwaysPreTouch touches that whole heap. Leave disk for two full copies.

./scripts/stop.sh
./scripts/measure-compact-headers.sh --world server/parkour-spiral

The argument is the world directory, the folder that contains level.dat. server/parkour-spiral is the usual map. Java 25 and server/paper.jar have to be on the host. Paper 26.3 will not start on an older JDK.

What it refuses

A copy taken while the world is open, or a server whose level is the original, is not a before and after. The harness checks the copy after cp and again immediately before Java starts. It refuses when:

  • the work directory is the original world, sits inside it, or contains it, including a symlink whose target is the world
  • the work directory is the live server/ directory
  • the copy's level.dat is missing, is a symlink, or is the same inode as the original
  • any symlink inside the copy points at the original world
  • any hardlink inside the copy is a file in the original world
  • Paper is still running from server/server.pid and the world sits inside that server directory
  • the original level.dat checksum changes during the two runs

A session.lock in the original world prints a warning. The same check is available for a copy made by hand:

./scripts/measure-compact-headers.sh check-copy \
    --source server/parkour-spiral \
    --dest /tmp/parkour-copy

Exit 1 means the harness refused to run, or a server did not finish. Exit 0 means a comparison was written, including a rejection.

What a passing run has to show

After warmup the harness samples used heap with jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info, falling back to jstat -gc, every 15 seconds through the soak. Pauses before the warmup mark are ignored, so startup GC stays out of the comparison. Then it sends tps and mspt on the console and stops the server.

The 1 minute TPS figure is the one that counts. A * from Paper means that window is not full yet, and the verdict is inconclusive. MSPT is the 1 minute average. TPS is capped at 20, so a slower tick can sit behind a perfect TPS number. MSPT is part of "TPS no worse".

The summary lands in .compact-headers-measure/<timestamp>/summary.md. latest points at that directory when the default work directory is used. verdict.txt is one word: ACCEPT, REJECT, or INCONCLUSIVE.

Enable the flag in scripts/jvm-opts.sh and in Compose JVM_XX_OPTS only when the copy shows a smaller heap and pauses and TPS are no worse:

  • Heap. The first sample after warmup and the high-water mark during the soak are both strictly lower with the flag.
  • GC pauses. Soak max and p99 are less than or equal to the baseline. Zero pauses on both sides counts as equal. G1's target in the current flags is -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200.
  • TPS. The 1 minute TPS is greater than or equal to the baseline, with a 0.05 tolerance so one decimal place from Paper is not a false failure.
  • MSPT. The 1 minute average is less than or equal to the baseline, with the same 0.05 ms tolerance.

ACCEPT means those gates passed. If the high-water drop is under 1%, the summary says to repeat the run before treating it as a real win. REJECT means leave the flag out. INCONCLUSIVE means a heap sample, a pause log, TPS, or MSPT was missing. One pair of idle soaks is noisy. A few milliseconds of pause jitter is a reason to run it again.

The numbers are still to come

I have not run this on parkour-spiral. That soak needs Java 25 and the world on the host, with the live server stopped, and it has not happened. tests/jvm-opts.sh checks the flag is absent by default and present when COMPACT_OBJECT_HEADERS is set, and that an unknown value fails. tests/compact-headers.sh checks the copy refusals (same path, symlink, hardlink, path overlap, and a live server.pid) and the ACCEPT / REJECT / INCONCLUSIVE parser, including a stubbed two-run measurement that never uses the original directory as the server world. Heap, pause, TPS, and MSPT numbers come from a real soak, and that soak has not been run.

The comparison is tracked on minecraft-server#129. When summary.md exists I will put it there. Until then the flag stays off.

entry.title: Why my radio app dipped to 1/14 volume on every network blip
entry.summary: In ShoutKit I fade player.volume in from silence when a station rejoins, so the live edge does not arrive as a click. A buffer underrun reports .playing again, and the rejoin fade treated that as a fresh start. The stream came back at full volume, the fade waited one step, then set the volume to 1/14 and swelled back to full. shoutkit#274 runs the fade only after the player was silenced.
entry.content:
In ShoutKit I fade player.volume in from silence when a station rejoins, so the live edge does not arrive as a click. A buffer underrun reports .playing again, and the rejoin fade treated that as a fresh start. The stream came back at full volume, the fade waited one step, then set the volume to 1/14 and swelled back to full. shoutkit#274 runs the fade only after the player was silenced.

The rejoin fade

Live radio has no position to resume. After an interruption, a stall, or a dropped connection, playback rejoins the stream at the live edge. The first decoded frames at full volume read as a click or a jump-cut, so since 2026-08-20 silenceForUpcomingPlayback() has set player.volume to zero in start, resume, and replayCurrentStream, and fadeInVolume() has brought it back over 350 ms once AudioStreaming reports .playing.

The ramp is fourteen steps. The task sleeps, then sets player.volume to Float(step) / Float(steps). The first assignment is 1/14. The last is 1.

static let volumeRampDuration = Duration.milliseconds(350)
static let volumeRampSteps = 14

let steps = Self.volumeRampSteps
let stepDuration = Self.volumeRampDuration / steps
for step in 1 ... steps {
    try? await Task.sleep(for: stepDuration)
    guard Task.isCancelled == false else { return }
    self.player.volume = Float(step) / Float(steps)
}

On a rejoin the volume was just zeroed, so that first step is silence becoming audible. On a player that is already at full volume, the same assignment is a dip.

A buffer underrun reports .playing

audioPlayerStateChanged calls fadeInVolume() on every transition into .playing:

case .playing:
    self.fadeInVolume()
    self.reportStatus(.playing, generation: generation)

AudioStreaming also enters .playing when a buffer underrun ends. Nothing on that path calls silenceForUpcomingPlayback(), so the player is already at full volume. The old fadeInVolume() still cancelled any ramp in flight, waited one step, set the volume to 1/14, and climbed back to 1. On ordinary network jitter during a long listen, the stream returned and then dipped.

The cancel is its own problem. A .playing that arrives while a rejoin fade is still running would stop the task and leave player.volume wherever the ramp had reached, then start again at 1/14. Coming back from an underrun has to leave a fade that is already running alone.

Arm the fade only after silence

silenceForUpcomingPlayback() still zeroes the volume, and it is the only call that arms a fade. fadeInVolume() runs the fourteen steps only when that arm is set. An unarmed .playing returns before it can cancel the task.

func silenceForUpcomingPlayback() {
    volumeRampTask?.cancel()
    volumeRampTask = nil
    volumeRampArm.arm()
    player.volume = 0
}

func fadeInVolume() {
    guard volumeRampArm.consume() else { return }
    volumeRampTask?.cancel()
    volumeRampTask = Task { @MainActor [weak self] in
        guard let self else { return }
        let steps = Self.volumeRampSteps
        let stepDuration = Self.volumeRampDuration / steps
        for step in 1 ... steps {
            try? await Task.sleep(for: stepDuration)
            guard Task.isCancelled == false else { return }
            self.player.volume = Float(step) / Float(steps)
        }
    }
}

consume() answers true once, then false until the next arm():

mutating func consume() -> Bool {
    defer { isArmed = false }
    return isArmed
}

start, resume, and replayCurrentStream still call silenceForUpcomingPlayback() first, so a real rejoin still fades in. VolumeRampArmTests covers the arm: consume() is false, true once after arm(), and false again. The fade and the arm live in AudioStreamingPlaybackEngine+VolumeRamp.swift. The .playing case is in audioPlayerStateChanged.

Also in that pull request

A station re-sends the current StreamTitle for the whole song, often about once a metadata interval, including while the app is backgrounded. When the lookup had produced neither artwork nor an Apple Music link, each repeat published again. That publication calls onTrackHeard, which writes listening history on the main actor, so a song the catalog does not know was a SwiftData fetch and save at that interval. The lookup still retries. An unchanged answer does not write history or the lock screen again. The first miss still publishes, because that .resolved push releases the artwork hold taken at the track boundary.

Old Shoutcast responses put their real headers in the body. ICYInBodyHeaders runs only when the HTTP response has two headers or fewer. It was ported from AudioStreaming's IcycastHeadersProcessor on 2026-11-14, including the part that passed each unfinished chunk straight through as audio. URLSession chooses the chunk sizes, so the first callback was often shorter than the block and was played as audio. A body that started with ICY or HTTP and never sent a blank line kept every later byte for the rest of the session. The reader now holds bytes only while they might still be a header. A single audio byte that cannot be ICY or HTTP is returned immediately. At 8 KB with no blank line, the buffer is released and treated as audio.

entry.title: http.Server.Shutdown doesn't cancel request contexts
entry.summary: In lazydeck, I gave serve one 30 second deadline for the HTTP drain and for reaping in-flight jobs. http.Server.Shutdown waits until handlers return. It leaves their request contexts alone. An open GET /v1/jobs/{id}/events stream sat in that wait long enough to expire the deadline, so the job reap cancelled the job and returned without waiting. execute was still blocked in cmd.Run. The uv, python, ssh, and rsync children are in their own process group, so they kept running after the process exited.
entry.content:
In lazydeck, I gave serve one 30 second deadline for the HTTP drain and for reaping in-flight jobs. http.Server.Shutdown waits until handlers return. It leaves their request contexts alone. An open GET /v1/jobs/{id}/events stream sat in that wait long enough to expire the deadline, so the job reap cancelled the job and returned without waiting. execute was still blocked in cmd.Run. The uv, python, ssh, and rsync children are in their own process group, so they kept running after the process exited.

One deadline, two waits

shutdownBudget was the whole shutdown, drain and then reap:

// shutdownBudget bounds how long Run waits, in total, for the HTTP server's
// graceful shutdown and then for in-flight jobs to actually cancel their
// SSH/rsync subprocess (see internal/client/process_unix.go's own 10s
// WaitDelay backstop) before Run returns anyway.
const shutdownBudget = 30 * time.Second

Run built one context from it and passed that context to both steps:

case <-ctx.Done():
    shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), shutdownBudget)
    defer cancel()
    for _, srv := range servers {
        if err := srv.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
            log.Printf("lazydeck serve: graceful HTTP shutdown failed: %v", err)
        }
    }
    // Cancel and wait for in-flight jobs even if HTTP shutdown above
    // didn't finish cleanly: otherwise a deploy's rsync/ssh could keep
    // running detached after this process has already returned/exited.
    if err := apiServer.jobs.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
        log.Printf("lazydeck serve: in-flight job(s) did not finish before shutdown timed out: %v", err)
        return err
    }

The reap does cancel every tracked job. Then it waits for the goroutines, or for the context, whichever comes first:

for _, j := range jobs {
    j.cancel()
}

done := make(chan struct{})
go func() {
    m.wg.Wait()
    close(done)
}()
select {
case <-done:
    return nil
case <-ctx.Done():
    return ctx.Err()
}

When the stream holds the drain for the whole 30 seconds, that shared context is already expired. The select takes ctx.Done() and returns ctx.Err() while execute is still inside cmd.Run. The cancel has been signaled. The wait never runs, and the process is free to exit.

The stream that held the drain

Shutdown closes listeners, closes idle connections, and waits for the rest to return to idle. A job event stream is in the middle of a response. Its handler returns when the request context ends.

BaseContext is the parent of incoming request contexts. Left nil, that parent is context.Background(). Cancelling the serve context does not reach the stream, so the stream holds Shutdown until the 30 second context expires. The reap then runs on that same context.

Both servers now derive request contexts from the serve context:

// Parent every request context on the serve context.
// http.Server.Shutdown does not cancel handlers; it only waits for them
// to return. Job SSE streams block in that wait until the request
// context ends, so without this they hold Shutdown until the deadline.
requestBase := func(net.Listener) context.Context { return ctx }
loopbackSrv := &http.Server{
    Handler:           apiServer.Handler(),
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 10 * time.Second,
    BaseContext:       requestBase,
}

The network server sets the same BaseContext. Cancelling serve cancels the stream's request context, the handler returns, and the connection can go idle.

HTTP still drains first, on its own 30 second budget, so a handler inside Submit publishes the job before jobs.Shutdown waits. A handler that ignores cancellation can still consume that whole budget. The reap gets a new one, and it waits:

httpCtx, httpCancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), shutdownBudget)
defer httpCancel()
for _, srv := range servers {
    if err := srv.Shutdown(httpCtx); err != nil {
        log.Printf("lazydeck serve: graceful HTTP shutdown failed: %v", err)
    }
}
jobCtx, jobCancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), shutdownBudget)
defer jobCancel()
if err := apiServer.jobs.Shutdown(jobCtx); err != nil {
    log.Printf("lazydeck serve: in-flight job(s) did not finish before shutdown timed out: %v", err)
    return err
}

That wait is what lets the process-group kill finish before exit. configureCancellation in internal/client/process_unix.go starts the child in its own group and, on cancel, signals the group:

func configureCancellation(cmd *exec.Cmd) {
    if cmd.SysProcAttr == nil {
        cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{}
    }
    cmd.SysProcAttr.Setpgid = true
    cmd.WaitDelay = cancelWaitDelay
    cmd.Cancel = func() error {
        return killProcessGroup(cmd)
    }
}

cancelWaitDelay is 10 seconds. killProcessGroup is syscall.Kill(-cmd.Process.Pid, syscall.SIGKILL), the group. uv execs Python, which shells out to ssh and rsync. Those grandchildren survive the serve process exiting, because they are not in its group. Waiting until cmd.Run returns is what reaps them.

TestRunShutdownWaitsForInFlightJobWithEventStreamOpen holds GET /v1/jobs/{id}/events open. Its client blocks in Deploy until the job context is cancelled, then sleeps 200 milliseconds. Run has to return within 5 seconds, and only after that sleep. The old path can sit in Shutdown for the full 30 seconds while the stream is open, so the test fails on the previous shutdown code and passes with this change. The pull request's go test -race ./... was clean with a stub uv on PATH. That environment has no uv.

The fix is lazydeck#125 (408c5ca).

Quitting the TUI leaked the same way

I started the TUI's device commands from context.Background(): status, register, deploy, sync-logs, delete, list-games, discover, connection info, and custom commands. Deploy looked like this:

ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Minute)
defer cancel()
err := cli.Deploy(ctx, dev.Machine, dev.Login, name, dir, false, nil)

q and Ctrl+C returned from Bubble Tea's Run without cancelling those contexts and without waiting. The children sit in their own process group, so they outlived the process too.

They now share one context, created with context.WithCancel and stored on the model. Each command's timeout is a child of that context. q and Ctrl+C cancel it, then quit:

case "ctrl+c", "q":
    if m.gate != nil {
        m.gate.cancel()
    }
    return m, tea.Quit

Bubble Tea still returns without joining the command goroutines. main waits after Run:

_, err = p.Run()
// Bubble Tea returns without joining command goroutines. Cancel any
// still in flight and wait until their process groups exit.
m.Shutdown()
return err

Shutdown cancels that context again and waits. Spinner and auto-refresh ticks are not in the wait, or it would sit on a timer. The cap is 15 seconds, past the client's 10 second WaitDelay after SIGKILL:

// commandShutdownBudget outlasts the client's 10s WaitDelay after SIGKILL,
// so a descendant holding a pipe open is reaped before the process exits.
const commandShutdownBudget = 15 * time.Second

Custom commands already set Setpgid and SIGKILL the group on cancel, same as the client. Their WaitDelay is 2 seconds.

TestQuitTerminatesCustomCommandProcessGroup runs a shell that backgrounds sleep 120 and checks the grandchild is gone after quit and Shutdown.

A panic skipped finish

In the same change, a panic inside a job's run function skipped finish. The job stayed running, so it was never pruned, and a client watching its event stream waited. The device lock was still released, because releaseDevice is deferred.

execute now recovers, logs the panic value, and finishes the job as failed. The job error is a fixed internal message. The panic text stays in the log. finish still runs the completion hook:

defer func() {
    rec := recover()
    if rec == nil {
        return
    }
    log.Printf("lazydeck: job %s panicked: %v", job.ID, rec)
    m.finish(job, Failed, "failed", &Error{
        Kind:    "internal",
        Message: "the devkit operation failed unexpectedly; see the lazydeck serve process log for details",
    })
}()

finish also prunes terminal jobs. Queued and running jobs cannot be evicted, so a burst past the cap used to sit until some later Submit. The cap is still 500.

TestRunPanicFinishesAndReleasesTheDevice panics with boom secret, checks the job is failed with kind internal, and checks that neither word is in the job error. TestPruneOnFinishDropsTerminalJobsWithoutAnotherSubmit fills the manager past the cap, lets the jobs finish, and expects only 500 to remain with no further submit.

This is lazydeck#126 (c8a1fab).

If a handler can outlive the deadline you also use to reap subprocesses, give the reap its own context and wait until the goroutine that owns the process has returned. Parent long-lived request contexts on a context you cancel when those handlers should leave. Shutdown will keep waiting until they do.

entry.title: Bad publisher feeds were opening the circuit breaker for iTunes
entry.summary: Five broken publisher feeds in a row used to open the circuit breaker in podr-service for 30 seconds. Search (/?q=), top podcasts (/?q=toppodcasts), and /podcast/{id} share that breaker with iTunes and Podcast Index, so they returned 500, or a cached entry still inside ttl + STALE_SECONDS. The log called the publisher failure an iTunes API error.
entry.content:
Five broken publisher feeds in a row used to open the circuit breaker in podr-service for 30 seconds. Search (/?q=), top podcasts (/?q=toppodcasts), and /podcast/{id} share that breaker with iTunes and Podcast Index, so they returned 500, or a cached entry still inside ttl + STALE_SECONDS. The log called the publisher failure an iTunes API error.

One CircuitBreaker lives on the Worker isolate. /health reports it as circuitBreaker. failure() opens it at failures >= 5, and the open state rests for 30 seconds. With podcastSummaries on, detail also fetches the iTunes feedUrl through rss_description(), on the same cached upstream as search, top, and detail. get() defaults proxy to True, so a status of 400 or more was raised as iTunes API error. rss_description() logs that and returns no summary. except Exception still called failure(), and a 200 called success(), which cleared the counter and closed the breaker. feed() already skipped CachedUpstream. Its docstring says a caller-supplied URL must not take iTunes down with it.

Only count failures of the dependency the breaker protects

I stopped counting those fetches in podr-service#719 (bed0cd3). They still use the cache. breaker=False skips failure() and success().

Before:

response, _ = await self.upstream.get(url, TTL_DETAIL, header_only=True)

provider = "iTunes" if proxy else "Podcast Index"
raise UpstreamError(f"{provider} API error: {response.status} {response.reason}")

except Exception:
    self.circuit.failure()
    raise
self.circuit.success()

After, same commit. The comment is on the call in rss_description():

# The URL belongs to the publisher. Counting it on the shared breaker
# would let a few broken feeds rest iTunes and Podcast Index, and the
# failure is not an error from either API.
response, _ = await self.upstream.get(url, TTL_DETAIL, header_only=True, breaker=False)

if breaker:
    provider = "iTunes" if proxy else "Podcast Index"
    label = f"{provider} API error"
else:
    label = "Feed error"
raise UpstreamError(f"{label}: {response.status} {response.reason}")

except asyncio.CancelledError:
    if probe:
        self.circuit.cancel_probe()
    raise
except Exception:
    if breaker:
        self.circuit.failure()
    raise
if breaker:
    self.circuit.success()

breaker defaults to True, so search, top, and detail still move it. A publisher 404 is now Feed error: 404. A connect error or a read timeout raises as itself, and rss_description() still logs RSS description unavailable. The new test sends 404, 500, 503, a connect error, a read timeout, and 502, then checks the breaker is "closed", failures is 0, and /?q=python returns 200. A successful fetch leaves a count of 4 where it was, and leaves an open breaker open. iTunes and Podcast Index still share the field /health reports, so an outage on either side can still rest the other.

Half-open should admit one probe

The old is_open() checked the rest and let callers through. get() fetches when it returns false:

def is_open(self):
    if self.state == "open" and time.time() - self.last_failure >= 30:
        self.state = "half-open"
    return self.state == "open"

The call that ends the 30 seconds sets "half-open" and gets false back. Every later caller does too, because the return is self.state == "open". They hit upstream together.

is_open() now only answers. "half-open" stays off upstream, and so does "open" while time.time() - self.last_failure < 30. A fresh cache hit returns from get() before _fetch, so the probe stays available. The test uses a fresh entry with last_failure 31 seconds ago and checks the state is still "open" with no upstream call. The next miss is the probe.

admit() reserves that one attempt, and it does not await:

def admit(self):
    """Reserve one upstream attempt. Half-open keeps the rest waiting."""
    if self.state == "closed":
        return True
    if self.state == "open" and time.time() - self.last_failure >= 30:
        self.state = "half-open"
        return True
    return False

A second request during the probe gets 500 and Service temporarily unavailable, with one upstream call. failure() on a failed probe sets last_failure to now and opens the breaker again, because the state is "half-open". The following request does not call upstream. The pull request's 503 case checks that.

A cancelled probe has no result to count. cancel_probe() returns the state to "open" and leaves last_failure where it was:

def cancel_probe(self):
    """The probe ended without a result. Leave the rest window where it was."""
    if self.state == "half-open":
        self.state = "open"

Otherwise the breaker would sit in "half-open". is_open() keeps later callers off upstream there, and admit() only starts a probe from "open".

The docstring on is_open() says this needs no lock. admit() does not await, and a Worker isolate has one event loop, so a second caller cannot pass admit() before the state is "half-open". On a cache miss, get() calls admit() before it awaits the fetch. While the breaker is "closed", admit() returns immediately and concurrent misses each still fetch. refreshing de-duplicates revalidation only on the Podcasts object fetch() builds per request.

Only count failures of the dependency the breaker protects. Half-open should admit one probe.

entry.title: I Made My Track Solver a Third Faster Without Changing One Answer
entry.summary: I'm building a racing game in Rust and Godot, a sibling to Salt Line. Every track in it is generated, and every generated track is proven drivable before a player sees it. Proving is slow: a late track costs about four million physics ticks, and a phone does that while the player looks at a menu.
entry.content:
I'm building a racing game in Rust and Godot, a sibling to Salt Line. Every track in it is generated, and every generated track is proven drivable before a player sees it. Proving is slow: a late track costs about four million physics ticks, and a phone does that while the player looks at a menu.

I took 36 percent off the proving time. The solver accepts the same tracks, sets the same timers and reports the same failures as before, bit for bit. Here's how I found the time, and how I know nothing moved.

The Short Version

BeforeAfter
Batch of 54 tracks, one thread9.15 s5.8 s
Mean per track (360 tracks)164 ms106 ms
Slowest track (360 tracks)1,183 ms724 ms
Custom layout proof, median36 ms21 ms
Solver resultsidentical

Those are from a 4-core x86-64 cloud machine, release build. I haven't measured a phone yet.

What "Proven" Costs

A human-like bot drives the track sixteen times to set the checkpoint timer. A perfect bot drives it to find the best possible time, searching which corners to drift. A grip-only bot checks that each drift corner really needs a drift. Then the human-like bot drives it sixteen more times on every car the player could own by that point. A track that fails any of this is redrawn and the whole thing starts again.

The sim is deterministic across Linux, macOS, Windows and phones, and a daily run has to be the same tracks for everyone. So the rule for this work was strict: an optimisation that moves one timer by a quarter second isn't an optimisation. It's a different game.

Save the Answers Before the First Edit

Before I touched anything, I saved the outputs I'd later diff against:

  • the full report of a 40-seed batch: 360 tracks, with every accepted draw, rejection reason and margin
  • the bundled courses, re-proven
  • a survey of custom layouts
  • the cross-platform determinism digest

After every change I ran them again and diffed, ignoring only the timing columns. That turned "I think this is equivalent" into a check that takes seconds.

Where the Time Went

I profiled with callgrind, since perf wasn't available on the machine. The split was nearly even: 52 percent in the perfect bot's drift search, 46 percent in human trials. Per tick, three things stood out:

  • 21 percent building the list of obstacles ahead of the car.
  • 9.5 percent in floor. On x86-64 without SSE4.1, f64::floor is a library call, and finding the road segment under the car made it several times a tick.
  • The human bot's look-ahead took a square root for every segment it could see, about thirty a tick.

Cheaper Ticks

A floor that wasn't needed

The segment index is floor(z / 4), clamped to the track. At or past the first segment boundary, truncating to an integer is the floor. Below it, the answer is zero.

let q = z / SEG_LEN;
if q < 1.0 {
    0
} else {
    (q as u32 as usize).min(self.segments.len() - 1)
}

The cast goes through u32 on purpose. Rust's float-to-integer casts saturate, and the saturating cast to usize is a longer instruction sequence than the one to u32. The clamp to the track length hides the difference.

A test checks the new form against the old one at every segment edge, at NaN, at both infinities and past 2⁶³.

Stop dividing

A track is stored as small integers: milliradians of curve, centimetres of width. That's what makes it identical everywhere and cheap to hash. But the car, the race and the bots were converting those integers to metres on every tick. The track now keeps the converted floats beside the integers. They're the same expressions, computed once, so they're the same bits.

This was the change the profiler undersold. Callgrind counts instructions, and a division is one instruction. The stopwatch said 6 percent.

One square root instead of thirty

The human bot wants the lowest of sqrt(limit² + 2·decel·d) over the road it can see. IEEE-754 square root is exactly rounded, and an exactly rounded function of one variable is monotonic: it can't reorder two values. So the root of the lowest is the lowest root, bit for bit. I take the minimum of the squares and then one root.

Fewer Ticks

Don't choose from one

Before setting the timer, the solver finds the weakest car the track can be met with, by running the perfect bot's full drift search on each. On the first two tracks of a run, and on every custom layout, there is exactly one car. The search ran anyway.

Don't search twice

With several cars, the weakest one's search ran before the track had a timer, and then again after. The bot never reads the timer. So a timer can change a search in only one way: by stopping one of its drives, which then ranks last.

I record how late the search's drives reached each checkpoint. If the calibrated timer would have stopped none of them, a second search would make the same drives and pick the same plan, so I skip it and drive the plan once. If it would have stopped one, I search again as before. A test runs both paths against a full search on generated tracks, with timers from barely enough to generous.

Don't re-plan the plan you have
